newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian meeting discusses economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian meeting discusses economic reform.

text.p: Hundreds of Nigerian businessmen and officials from the military government gathered in the capital Abuja on Thursday to discuss ways to reform the country's stagnant economy.
Delegates to the "Economic Summit" were to debate macroeconomic policy, trade and investment in the long and short term before making recommendations to the government.
Previous summits are credited with influencing Nigeria's military ruler, General Sani Abacha, to carry out a "guided deregulation" policy over the past two years.

"The time of direct government involvement in business is over and by the same token the time has passed when the private sector looked up to government for all the infrastructure needed for business," Abacha said on Wednesday.
Despite the billions which Africa's most populous nation has earned through crude oil sales, its economy has spiralled into ever deeper decline.
Economic policies have often stifled rather than accelerated growth as successive military governments abruptly changed priorities.

"The military are not exactly experts in these fields, but at least if they are listening to us then some of our ideas might filter through and bear fruit," said one private sector delegate who preferred not to be named.
While liberalisation has swept much of the continent, Nigeria has kept more firmly to interventionist policies.
Although the government has liberalised foreign exchange and repealed controls on external investment, it has paid little more than lip service to other reforms.
"The key changes we've had since 1993 were recommended by the economic summit and are already having a major impact," Ibrahim Ida, economic adviser to the president, told reporters.
Hindering a medium-term economic plan, essential for talks on rescheduling a $32 billion debt, are the dual exchange rate, interest rate caps and subsidies on fuel and fertiliser.
Finance Minister Anthony Ani told delegates the government was ready to abolish the dual exchange rate and fertiliser subsidy, even going as far as to suggest eventual divestment from oil production.
But at the same time he spoke of continued commitment to developing the steel industry, in which an estimated $8 billion has been invested over the last 20 years without concrete results.
Delegates from the private sector are pushing for the stalled privatisation programme to be restarted or at least for competition to be permitted in key areas.

"We urge that the private sector be allowed to operate...even in areas such as telecommunications, power and oil refineries, where outside privatisation seems untouchable," said Pascal Dozie, president of the Nigerian Stock Exchange.
"The private sector should be allowed to participate even if only to force existing parastatals (state-owned companies) in these areas to improve their service quality," he added.
